entries.title: Amandine
entries.summary: Amandine is fish cooked the meunière way and finished with flaked almonds toasted golden in brown butter, with lemon and parsley. It is the method behind New Orleans's trout amandine, and the template for the Louisiana habit of putting pecans in the pan.
entries.guest: Amandine means finished with almonds: the fish is sautéed golden in butter, then topped with almonds toasted in brown butter, with lemon and parsley.

paras: Amandine, from the French amande, almond, is a finish rather than a sauce of its own. The fish is first cooked à la meunière, the miller's wife's way: seasoned, dusted in flour and sautéed golden. Then flaked almonds are toasted in fresh butter until the butter turns hazelnut brown and the almonds pale gold, lemon juice and chopped parsley go in at the last moment, and the foaming panful is spooned over the fish. The almonds bring crunch and a sweet, toasted flavour that a plain meunière lacks.

In New Orleans a favourite plate is trout amandine, made with speckled trout, a Gulf fish of the drum family rather than a freshwater trout. American menus often spell it almondine, an anglicised form of the French word. Both mean the same plate, and a cook should recognise either on a ticket.

Season the fillets, dredge them in flour and shake off every bit of excess. Sauté them in clarified butter, butter with its water and milk solids taken out so it takes the heat without burning, over medium-high heat until golden on both sides, a few minutes for a thin fillet, and lift them onto a warm plate. Pour off the fat and wipe the pan, or take a second one, because flour left behind burns as the butter browns.

Put the pan over medium heat with fresh whole butter. When it foams, add the almonds and keep them moving so every flake colours evenly. Within a minute or two the foam settles, the milk solids turn brown and the butter smells of hazelnuts; the almonds should be pale gold to light brown. Off the heat, add the lemon juice, which hisses and stops the browning, then the parsley and a pinch of salt. Spoon it over the fish at once, while it still foams.

Busy kitchens often toast the almonds ahead on a tray in the oven, at about 160 to 175°C (320 to 347°F) for 5 to 8 minutes, then warm them through in the browning butter to order. The nuts colour evenly and the line moves faster.

For one portion of 170 to 200 g (6 to 7 oz) of fish, allow about 30 g (1 oz) of butter for the sauce, 20 to 25 g (about 3/4 oz) of flaked almonds, 1 to 2 tsp (5 to 10 ml) of lemon juice and a spoonful of chopped parsley. Flaked almonds, cut thin, toast faster and more evenly than slivered or whole ones.

Almonds go from golden to burnt in seconds and keep cooking in the hot butter after the pan leaves the heat, so pull them a shade lighter than you want them. Burnt nuts taste bitter and cannot be saved: start again. A soggy coat on the fish comes from wet fillets, too much flour or a pan that was not hot enough. Black specks in the sauce are flour left from the sauté. Parsley added too early wilts and darkens, and butter left without its lemon goes on browning towards burnt.

The same logic works with other nuts. Louisiana cooks put pecans in the pan in exactly the same way, a toasted pecan butter spooned over sautéed or fried fish, and hazelnuts or pistachios turn up on modern menus. The method fits any thin, white, delicate fillet that takes a meunière well: sole, flounder, drum or trout.

No amandine appears on the menus the house guide covers. The nearest cousin is the Pecan Gulf Fish: today's Gulf fish with lump crab and a pecan bordelaise. In New Orleans bordelaise usually means garlic butter rather than the French red wine sauce, and the guide reads this one as garlic butter with toasted pecans worked in: nuts and butter over fish, the Louisiana swap. That is a reading, not a recipe, so confirm at lineup which bordelaise it is.

Describe amandine plainly: fish sautéed golden in butter, with almonds toasted in brown butter, lemon and parsley spooned over. Almonds are tree nuts and they toast in the same butter that sauces the fish, so a nut allergy question goes straight to the kitchen, which alone decides whether a separate, clean pan and fresh butter are possible. Never promise it yourself.

faults.cause: The pan was too hot, the nuts sat still, or they went in after the butter had already browned.
faults.fix: Start again, because burnt nuts cannot be saved. Toast them in foaming butter over medium heat and keep them moving, or toast them ahead in the oven.

faults.cause: Pulled too soon, or crowded into a pan too small to colour them evenly.
faults.fix: Toast them in a single layer a little longer, or toast them ahead on a tray in the oven.

faults.fault: Soggy, greasy coating on the fish
faults.cause: Wet fillets, too much flour, or fat that was not hot when the fish went in.
faults.fix: Pat the fish dry, shake off the excess flour and heat the clarified butter before the fillets go in.

faults.fault: Black specks and an acrid sauce
faults.cause: Flour and old fat left in the pan from the sauté burned as the butter browned.
faults.fix: Wipe the pan, or use a second pan for the brown butter and almonds.

faults.cause: No lemon, or lemon and parsley added too early, so the parsley wilted and the butter kept browning.
faults.fix: Add the lemon off the heat at the last moment, then the parsley, and spoon it over at once.

brennans.how: Today's Gulf fish with lump crab and a pecan bordelaise, which the guide reads as New Orleans garlic butter with toasted pecans: nuts and butter over fish, as in an amandine. Confirm at lineup whether it is garlic butter or red wine. Nut and shellfish questions go to the kitchen.

questions.q: The almonds are golden, but the sauce is full of black specks and tastes acrid. What went wrong?
questions.answer: Flour left from the sauté burned
distractors: The almonds were toasted ahead in the oven
The lemon went in off the heat
The parsley went in at the last moment

questions.q: Why should the almonds come off the heat a shade lighter than you want them?
questions.answer: They keep browning in the hot butter
distractors: They darken further once the lemon goes in
Dark almonds sink in the sauce

questions.q: When does the lemon juice go into the brown butter for an amandine?
questions.answer: At the last moment, off the heat
distractors: At the start, with the cold butter
As soon as the almonds go in
questions.why: Lemon stops the browning and keeps the sauce bright, so it goes in off the heat once the butter is hazelnut brown; added with the cold butter it stops the colour before it starts.

questions.q: Speckled trout, the fish of a New Orleans trout amandine, belongs to which family of fish?
questions.why: Speckled trout, the spotted seatrout of the Gulf, is a drum, a cousin of the redfish, and not a true trout, whatever its name suggests.

questions.q: On an American menu, what does almondine mean?
questions.answer: The same almond finish as amandine
distractors: Almonds baked into a pastry crust
questions.why: Almondine is the anglicised spelling of amandine; both describe fish with almonds toasted in brown butter, lemon and parsley.

questions.q: What is the Louisiana swap on an amandine?

Cane syrup in place of lemon
questions.why: Louisiana cooks keep the logic and change the nut: pecans toasted in butter and spooned over the fish.

questions.q: Why does a nut allergy question about an amandine always go to the kitchen?
questions.answer: The nuts share the fish's pan and butter
distractors: So the almonds can be left off at the pass
Servers may not name any ingredient
The almonds are added at the table
questions.why: The almonds share the very pan and butter spooned over the fish, so only the kitchen can judge a separate, clean pan; a server never promises it.

questions.q: Which Brennan's dish puts nuts in the sauce over its fish, the nearest cousin on the menu to an amandine?
questions.why: The Pecan Gulf Fish carries a pecan bordelaise, which the guide reads as garlic butter with toasted pecans; whether it is garlic butter or red wine is confirmed at lineup.

questions.q: The almonds are in the foaming butter. Which sign says it is time for the lemon?
distractors: Smoke rises and the almonds darken
The foam climbs higher and turns white
The almonds sink to the bottom
questions.why: Once the foam settles, the butter smells of hazelnuts and the almonds are pale gold; smoke means it has gone too far, and rising white foam means water is still boiling off.

entries.title: Clarified butter
entries.summary: Clarified butter is butter with its water and milk solids taken away, leaving pure golden butterfat. It takes more heat than whole butter without burning, gives a firmer hollandaise and is the cooking fat of a meunière.
entries.guest: Clarified butter is butter melted gently and strained so only the pure golden fat remains; it gives fish a clean, buttery crust without burning.

paras: Butter is not all fat. American butter must by law be at least 80 per cent butterfat; most of the rest is water, about 16 per cent, with a little milk protein, milk sugar and sometimes salt, together called the milk solids. Clarifying separates them. Melted gently, the water cooks away or settles, the solids rise as foam or sink, and what remains is clear, golden butterfat, beurre clarifié in French.

It matters because the milk solids are what burn. Whole butter starts to smoke and scorch at around 150 to 175°C (302 to 347°F); clarified butter holds to roughly 200 to 250°C (392 to 482°F), the figure varying with the source and with how cleanly the butter was clarified. With no water left it does not spit in a hot pan, and it keeps far longer than whole butter.

Cooks reach for it in three places. It is the fat for sautéing fish à la meunière and anything else cooked hot in butter, because it browns the food without burning itself. It makes a thicker, steadier hollandaise than whole butter, which brings its own water. And with nothing to spit or scorch, it suits the crêpe pan and the pastry brush.

Use unsalted butter, so the seasoning stays in the cook's hands. Cut it into pieces and melt it over low heat, in a heavy pan, a bain-marie (a pan set in hot water) or a low oven. Let it bubble quietly without stirring: the water cooks off with a soft crackle, and a white foam of milk protein rises. Skim it away.

When the bubbling slows and the fat looks clear, take it off the heat and let it stand a few minutes. Ladle or pour the golden fat off the top, leave the milky layer at the bottom behind, and strain it through muslin (cheesecloth) for a clean finish. Another way: melt it, chill it until the fat sets into a disc, lift the disc off and discard the liquid beneath.
Expect about 75 to 80 per cent of the weight you started with: 450 g (1 lb) of butter gives roughly 340 to 360 g (about 12 oz) of clarified butter. Plan the order for that loss.

Ghee is the clarified butter of South Asian kitchens, taken one step further. The butter is cooked on after the water has gone, until the milk solids on the bottom turn golden brown and the fat smells nutty and toasted, then it is strained. It tastes deeper than plain clarified butter and is the everyday fat for frying spices, cooking rice and brushing breads. Because the browned solids are strained out, it is a cousin of brown butter, not the same thing.

Cloudy clarified butter still holds milk solids: let it settle and decant it again, more slowly, through muslin. Fat that spits still holds water and needed longer over the heat. If the heat was too high the solids brown and the fat tastes nutty, which suits some dishes but not a pale hollandaise. Clarified salted butter leaves most of its salt in the milky layer, but some carries over, so taste before seasoning.

On the station, clarified butter is kept liquid in a covered container or squeeze bottle in a warm spot, such as the back of the stove, with its own clean ladle. Flour from dredged fish, crumbs and used pan fat never go back in: they burn the next time the butter heats and spoil the whole batch. Label and date it, and follow the chef's rule for how long it stays out.

Guests meet it as drawn butter, the warm melted or clarified butter American menus serve with lobster, crab and steamed clams, and in the clean, golden crust of a meunière. A guest who asks whether clarified butter or ghee is still dairy is answered by the kitchen and the service note, never by a guess: both are made from butter.

faults.cause: Milk solids carried over: poured too fast, not left to settle or not strained.
faults.fix: Let it stand, then decant it again slowly and strain it through muslin.

faults.cause: Water is still in it, because it came off the heat too soon.
faults.fix: Return it to low heat until the bubbling stops, then decant and strain it.

faults.fault: Brown, nutty fat where clear was wanted
faults.cause: The heat was too high or it cooked too long, and the solids browned.
faults.fix: Use it where a nutty flavour suits; for a pale sauce, clarify a new batch over lower heat.

faults.cause: Flour, crumbs or used pan fat went back into the clean butter and burned.
faults.fix: Strain it or replace it, keep a clean ladle, and never pour used fat back.

cards.front: What is clarified butter?
cards.back: Butter melted gently so the water cooks off and the milk solids are skimmed or left behind, leaving pure golden butterfat.

cards.front: What is whole butter made of besides fat?
cards.back: About 16 per cent water, plus milk solids: protein, milk sugar and any salt. American butter must be at least 80 per cent butterfat.

cards.front: Why does whole butter burn sooner than clarified butter?
cards.back: Its milk solids scorch from around 150 to 175°C (302 to 347°F); with them gone, the pure fat holds to roughly 200°C (392°F) or more.

cards.front: How is butter clarified in a kitchen?
cards.back: Melt it slowly, let the water bubble off, skim the foam, then ladle the clear fat off the milky layer and strain it through muslin.

cards.front: How much clarified butter does 450 g (1 lb) of whole butter give?
cards.back: About 75 to 80 per cent of its weight, roughly 340 to 360 g (about 12 oz), once the water and solids are gone.

cards.front: Besides taking the heat, why does clarified butter suit the hot pan of a meunière?
cards.back: With no water left it does not spit, and with no milk solids it browns the floured fish golden without burning itself.

cards.front: What does clarified butter do for a hollandaise?
cards.back: It makes a thicker, steadier sauce than whole butter, which brings its own water and loosens the emulsion.

cards.front: How does ghee differ from plain clarified butter?
cards.back: Ghee is cooked on until the milk solids brown, so the strained fat tastes nutty and toasted; plain clarified butter stays pale and clean.

cards.front: What is drawn butter on an American menu?
cards.back: Warm melted or clarified butter served for dipping lobster, crab or steamed clams.

cards.front: How is clarified butter kept on the station?
cards.back: Liquid, covered, in a warm spot with its own clean ladle; crumbs and used pan fat never go back in, and the chef's rule sets how long it stays out.

cards.front: Why do cooks clarify unsalted butter?
cards.back: So the cook keeps control of the seasoning; with salted butter some salt always carries over into the fat.

cards.front: Why does a guest's dairy question about ghee go to the kitchen?
cards.back: Ghee and clarified butter are both made from butter, so only the kitchen and the service note can answer for a guest, never a guess.

questions.q: What is left once butter has been clarified?
questions.why: Clarifying drives off the water and removes the milk solids, so only the golden butterfat remains.

questions.q: Why can clarified butter take more heat than whole butter?
distractors: It still holds all its water
questions.why: The milk solids are what burn in whole butter; without them the pure fat holds to roughly 200°C (392°F) or more before smoking.

questions.q: Roughly what share of whole butter's weight is left after clarifying?
questions.why: Butter is about 16 per cent water plus a little milk solid; take those away and about three quarters or a little more remains.

questions.q: Besides taking the heat, why does clarified butter suit the hot sauté pan of a meunière?
questions.answer: With no water left, it does not spit
distractors: It gives the fish a nutty brown flavour
It makes the flour coat cling thicker
It keeps the fish pale and soft inside
questions.why: Clarifying drives off the water, so the fat does not spit in the hot pan; with the milk solids gone it browns the floured fish without burning itself.

questions.q: How does clarified butter change a hollandaise, compared with whole butter?
distractors: A sauce that can never split
questions.why: Clarified butter is almost pure fat, so the same yolks set a thicker emulsion; it still splits if mistreated.

questions.q: What sets ghee apart from plain clarified butter?
questions.answer: Its solids brown before it is strained
distractors: Its browned solids are left in the fat
It is taken off as soon as it melts
It is churned again with water
questions.why: Ghee is cooked on after the water has gone until the milk solids brown, which gives the strained fat its nutty taste.

questions.q: On an American menu, what is drawn butter?
distractors: Butter piped into rosettes for bread
Butter worked with flour to thicken
Butter frozen into curls for the table
questions.why: Drawn butter is warm melted or clarified butter served for dipping lobster, crab and steamed clams.

questions.q: Why must crumbs and used pan fat never go back into the clarified butter on the station?
questions.answer: They burn and spoil the batch
distractors: They make it set too hard
questions.why: Solids burn the next time the butter heats, giving bitter specks to everything cooked in that batch.

questions.q: Why do cooks clarify unsalted butter rather than salted?
questions.answer: The cook keeps control of seasoning

entries.title: Compound butters
entries.summary: Compound butters, beurres composés in French, are softened butter worked with a flavouring, rolled, chilled and sliced. A disc melts over hot grilled meat or fish into an instant sauce; others, such as crustacean butter, finish classic sauces.
entries.guest: A compound butter is butter blended with herbs or other flavourings, chilled and sliced, so it melts over the hot food into a quick, rich sauce.

paras: A compound butter, beurre composé in French, is softened butter beaten with a flavouring, rolled into a log, chilled and sliced. A cold disc laid on a hot grilled steak or fish melts into a glossy, seasoned sauce on the way to the table, with no pan and no last-minute work. Escoffier listed a long run of them, some for grills and some for finishing sauces, and those two uses still divide the family.
For a Sous Chef they are mise en place, the work set out before service, that becomes a sauce: made in a quiet hour, sliced to order, and the same on the last plate as on the first.

Bring unsalted butter to a soft, spreadable texture, about 18 to 20°C (64 to 68°F), what French cooks call en pommade: soft enough to take a fingertip, nowhere near melting. Beat it smooth, then work in the flavourings, chopped fine and dry, then salt and pepper, and any acid last, a little at a time so the butter takes the liquid. Keep wet additions such as a reduction modest, or the butter weeps.

Spoon the butter in a line along parchment or cling film (plastic wrap), roll it into a tight cylinder about 3 cm (about 1 1/4 inches) across, twist the ends and chill until firm. Slice discs to order with a knife dipped in hot water and dried, or freeze the logs and cut from frozen.

Crustacean butter, beurre de crustacés, is the exception, often made hot. The shells of lobster, crayfish or shrimp are pounded or blitzed with butter and heated gently until the fat turns coral red and smells of the sea, then strained through cloth into iced water, where the coloured fat sets and is lifted off. It finishes sauce Nantua, béchamel (milk thickened with a roux of butter and flour) enriched with cream and finished with crayfish butter and crayfish tails, and sauce cardinal, which owes its red colour to lobster butter.

Maître d'hôtel butter is the classic: parsley, lemon juice, salt and pepper, on grilled steak and grilled fish. Bercy butter adds shallot reduced in white wine and diced, poached beef marrow, with parsley and lemon, for grilled steak. Colbert butter is maître d'hôtel butter with melted meat glaze, glace de viande, and chopped tarragon. Escargot butter, packed over snails in their shells and baked, is garlic, shallot and parsley beaten into butter.

Then there are house butters. Café de Paris butter takes its name from the Café de Paris in Geneva, which serves entrecôte, a rib steak, beneath it and still keeps the recipe secret; versions made elsewhere run to a long list of herbs, spices, mustard and capers. Many restaurants keep a signature butter of their own.

Butter too cold will not take its flavourings and stays lumpy and streaked. Butter too warm, or melted, turns greasy, the herbs sink and it sets grainy when chilled again. Wet herbs or a warm reduction weep beads of water and shorten the butter's life, so dry the herbs and cool every liquid first. Garlic and fresh herbs fade within days: keep the logs wrapped, labelled, dated and cold, and freeze what will not be used soon.

At Brennan's two compound butters finish dishes on the breakfast and lunch menu. Foie gras butter, foie gras puréed into soft butter, melts into the pockets of the cornbread waffle on the Duck Confit Waffle with the mustard maple syrup. House-made miso butter is miso, a fermented soybean paste, beaten into soft butter, salty, nutty and savoury; it rounds out the sweet crab and corn on the Crab & Corn Omelette, and because the guide names soy on this dish, dietary questions go to the service note and the kitchen.

Describe a compound butter by what is in it and what it does: herbs and lemon melting over a steak, foie gras melting into a waffle. Some guests avoid foie gras by choice, and the house guide asks you to check with the kitchen whether it can be left off before you promise it. Crustacean butter in a sauce, miso in a butter: every question about what a butter is made with goes to the service note and the kitchen.

faults.cause: The butter was too cold when the flavourings went in.
faults.fix: Let it soften to en pommade and beat it again until smooth.

faults.cause: The butter was too warm or melted, so its water separated and the flavourings sank.
faults.fix: Chill it until it just begins to firm, then beat it hard; if water has pooled, start again with softened butter.

faults.fault: Beads of water and a short life
faults.cause: Wet herbs, or a reduction added while still warm.
faults.fix: Dry the herbs well, cool every liquid first and keep wet additions modest.

faults.fix: Chill the log until firm and slice with a knife dipped in hot water and wiped dry.

brennans.how: Foie gras puréed into soft butter melts into the pockets of the cornbread waffle with the mustard maple syrup. Some guests avoid foie gras by choice: ask the kitchen whether it can be left off before promising it.

Miso, a fermented soybean paste, is beaten into soft butter to make a salty, nutty, savoury compound butter that rounds out the sweet crab and corn. Send any question about the miso to the service note and the kitchen.

cards.front: What is a compound butter?
cards.back: Softened butter worked with a flavouring, rolled into a log, chilled and sliced; a disc melts over hot food into an instant sauce.

cards.front: How soft should the butter be before the flavourings go in?
cards.back: En pommade: soft and spreadable, about 18 to 20°C (64 to 68°F), never melted, so it takes the flavourings and still sets.

cards.front: What goes into maître d'hôtel butter?
cards.back: Parsley, lemon juice, salt and pepper: the classic disc on grilled steak and grilled fish.

cards.front: What goes into Bercy butter?
cards.back: Shallot reduced in white wine, diced poached beef marrow, parsley and lemon, beaten into butter for grilled steak.

cards.front: How is Colbert butter built?
cards.back: On maître d'hôtel butter, with melted meat glaze, glace de viande, and chopped tarragon worked in.

cards.front: What is in escargot butter?
cards.back: Garlic, shallot and parsley beaten into butter, packed over snails in their shells and baked.

cards.front: Where does Café de Paris butter come from?
cards.back: The Café de Paris in Geneva, which serves entrecôte beneath it and still keeps its recipe secret.

cards.front: How is crustacean butter, beurre de crustacés, made?
cards.back: Shells are pounded with butter, heated until the fat turns coral red, strained through cloth into iced water, and the set fat lifted off.

cards.front: Which classic sauces are finished with crustacean butter?
cards.back: Sauce Nantua, with crayfish butter and crayfish tails, and sauce cardinal, which takes its red colour from lobster butter.

Brushed only on the raw meat
Melted in a jug on the side
questions.why: The disc is sliced cold from the log and laid on the hot meat, where it melts into an instant sauce at the table.

questions.q: How soft should the butter be when the flavourings are worked in?
questions.answer: Spreadable, still cool to the touch
distractors: Half melted, soft at the edges
questions.why: Butter en pommade takes the flavourings evenly and still sets firm; cold butter stays lumpy and melted butter turns greasy.

questions.q: Which flavourings make a maître d'hôtel butter?
questions.why: Maître d'hôtel is the plain classic of parsley, lemon juice, salt and pepper; Colbert builds on it with meat glaze and tarragon.

questions.q: Colbert butter is maître d'hôtel butter with which additions?
questions.why: Colbert adds melted glace de viande and chopped tarragon to the parsley and lemon of a maître d'hôtel butter.

questions.q: Which compound butter carries shallot, white wine and poached beef marrow?
questions.why: Bercy butter is built on shallot reduced in white wine with diced poached marrow, parsley and lemon, for grilled steak.

questions.q: Why is crustacean butter strained into iced water?
questions.answer: So the red fat sets on top
distractors: To cook the shells a second time
To wash the salt out of it
To whip air into the butter
questions.why: Cold water sets the red, flavoured fat on the surface, leaving shell fragments and liquid behind.

questions.q: Which sauce is finished with crayfish butter and crayfish tails?
questions.why: Sauce Nantua is a cream-enriched béchamel finished with crayfish butter and crayfish tails; cardinal takes lobster butter instead.

questions.q: In which city does the Café de Paris serve its secret butter over entrecôte?
questions.why: Despite the name, Café de Paris butter comes from Geneva, where the restaurant serves entrecôte beneath it and keeps the recipe secret.

questions.q: A compound butter was softened until it melted. What happens when it is chilled again?
distractors: It sets back exactly as it was
The flavourings rise and it sets smooth
questions.why: Melting breaks the butter's own emulsion, so its water separates, the flavourings sink and the texture turns grainy on chilling.

questions.q: A guest asks for the Duck Confit Waffle without the foie gras butter. What does the server do first?
questions.answer: Ask the kitchen before promising it
distractors: Promise it, since it is only butter
Offer miso butter in its place
questions.why: Some guests avoid foie gras by choice, and the house guide asks you to check with the kitchen whether it can be left off before you promise it.

entries.title: Mayonnaise
entries.summary: Mayonnaise is a cold emulsion of egg yolk and oil, seasoned with mustard and sharpened with vinegar or lemon. It is the cold cousin of hollandaise and the parent of rémoulade, tartare, verte and a family of cold sauces.
entries.guest: Mayonnaise is egg yolk whisked with oil, a little mustard and lemon or vinegar into a thick, cool sauce, the base of tartare sauce and the French rémoulade.

paras: Mayonnaise is a cold emulsion: tiny droplets of oil held apart in a little water, from the yolk and the vinegar or lemon juice. Lecithin and proteins in the yolk coat each droplet so the droplets cannot run back together, and their crowding is what makes the sauce thick. Mustard adds flavour and helps the emulsion form. No heat is involved: it is the cold cousin of hollandaise.

Escoffier treated it as a basic sauce, the parent of the cold sauces, doing for the cold kitchen what espagnole, the brown sauce, and velouté, the white stock sauce, do for the hot one. It is not among the four grandes sauces de base, the great base sauces, of his Guide (espagnole, velouté, béchamel and tomate), nor among the five mother sauces that later teaching made by adding hollandaise, but it stands beside them.

Have everything at room temperature: a cold yolk is slow to emulsify, and cold oil is thick and hard to break into droplets. Set the bowl on a damp cloth to steady it and whisk the yolk with the mustard, a pinch of salt and a few drops of vinegar or lemon juice.

Add the oil a drop at a time, whisking all the while, until the sauce thickens and turns pale: the emulsion has taken. Then pour in a thin, steady stream. As it stiffens, whisk in a few drops of water or lemon juice before adding more oil, because what runs out first is the water, not the yolk. Finish with acid and salt to taste. A food processor or stick blender works the same way, only faster.

Use a neutral oil such as sunflower, rapeseed (canola) or grapeseed. Olive oil brings flavour, but extra virgin olive oil beaten hard, above all in a blender, can turn bitter, so cooks use it for only part of the oil, whisked in by hand at the end.

One yolk comfortably holds roughly 150 to 250 ml of oil, with about 1 tsp (5 ml) of mustard and 1 to 2 tsp (5 to 10 ml) of vinegar or lemon juice. Escoffier worked at six yolks to 1 litre (about 1 quart) of oil, about 165 ml a yolk. A yolk can carry far more if water goes in as it thickens, but a working ratio leaves a margin.

From mayonnaise come rémoulade, with mustard, gherkins, capers, herbs and a little anchovy; tartare, today usually mayonnaise with chopped pickles, capers, onion and chives, though the classical one was mounted on hard-boiled yolks; verte, coloured green with a purée of blanched herbs and leaves such as spinach, watercress, tarragon and chervil; and andalouse, with tomato purée and fine strips of sweet red pepper. Aïoli and the New Orleans rémoulades, some built on mayonnaise and some on Creole mustard without it, have entries of their own.

A mayonnaise splits, turning thin, oily and curdled, when the oil goes in too fast before the emulsion has taken, when the ingredients are cold, or when too much oil is forced into too little water. To rescue it, put a fresh yolk, or a spoonful of water or mustard, in a clean bowl and whisk the broken sauce into it drop by drop, then in a stream. A sauce that is only too thick needs a few drops of water, not more oil.

The yolk in a mayonnaise is never cooked, and Salmonella can be inside an egg as well as on its shell. Restaurant kitchens therefore commonly make it with pasteurised eggs or yolks, heated just enough to kill bacteria without setting. Keep mayonnaise and everything made from it covered and cold, at 5°C (41°F) or below, and follow the kitchen's dating.

At the table, say what it is: egg yolk and oil whisked into a cool, thick sauce. What goes into any house sauce is the kitchen's answer, never a guess: the style of the chive rémoulade on the Crawfish Meat Pies is the kitchen's to say, as is any question about egg in a sauce.

ratios.label: Escoffier's proportion
ratios.value: 6 yolks to 1 litre (about 1 quart) of oil

ratios.label: Vinegar or lemon juice for each yolk

temps.label: Hold mayonnaise cold, at or below

faults.cause: Oil added too fast before the emulsion took, cold ingredients, or too much oil for the water.
faults.fix: Whisk the broken sauce drop by drop into a fresh yolk, or a spoonful of water or mustard, in a clean bowl.

faults.cause: The oil went in as a stream from the start, or the yolk was too cold.
faults.fix: Start a fresh base at room temperature and whisk the thin mixture into it slowly.

faults.cause: Too much oil for the water in the sauce.
faults.fix: Whisk in a few drops of water or lemon juice until it loosens.

faults.cause: Extra virgin olive oil beaten hard, especially in a blender.
faults.fix: Use a neutral oil for most of it and whisk the olive oil in by hand at the end.

cards.front: What kind of sauce is mayonnaise?
cards.back: A cold emulsion of egg yolk and oil, seasoned with mustard and sharpened with vinegar or lemon juice.

cards.front: What holds the oil droplets apart in a mayonnaise?
cards.back: Lecithin and proteins from the yolk coat each droplet in the little water present, so the droplets cannot merge.

cards.front: How much oil does one yolk comfortably hold?
cards.back: Roughly 150 to 250 ml; Escoffier worked at six yolks to 1 litre (about 1 quart), about 165 ml a yolk.

cards.front: Why does the oil go in drop by drop at the start?
cards.back: The emulsion has to take first; once the sauce thickens and turns pale, the oil can go in as a thin stream.

cards.front: Why should the yolk and oil be at room temperature?
cards.back: A cold yolk emulsifies slowly and cold oil is thick and hard to break into droplets, so a cold mayonnaise splits easily.

cards.front: The mayonnaise is stiff and there is oil still to add. What do you do?
cards.back: Whisk in a few drops of water or lemon juice first: the water runs out before the yolk does.

cards.front: Which oil suits mayonnaise, and why use olive oil only in part?
cards.back: A neutral oil; extra virgin olive oil beaten hard, especially in a blender, can turn bitter, so it is added for flavour, by hand.

cards.front: Name four cold sauces built on mayonnaise, and say where it stands beside the mother sauces.
cards.back: Rémoulade, tartare, verte with its green herb purée, and andalouse with tomato and sweet red pepper. Escoffier treated mayonnaise as the parent of the cold sauces, though it is neither one of his four grandes sauces nor one of the later five.

cards.front: A mayonnaise has split into a thin, oily curdle. How do you bring it back?
cards.back: Whisk a fresh yolk, or a spoonful of water or mustard, in a clean bowl, then whisk the broken sauce into it drop by drop, then in a stream.

cards.front: What does mustard do in a mayonnaise?
cards.back: It adds flavour and helps the emulsion form, its fine particles coating the oil droplets alongside the yolk.

cards.front: Why do restaurant kitchens commonly use pasteurised eggs for mayonnaise?
cards.back: The yolk is never cooked, and Salmonella can be inside an egg; pasteurising kills bacteria without setting the yolk.

cards.front: How is finished mayonnaise stored?
cards.back: Covered and cold, at 5°C (41°F) or below, with everything made from it, and dated by the kitchen's rule.

questions.q: What sets mayonnaise apart from hollandaise?
questions.answer: It is a cold emulsion made with oil
distractors: It is thickened with a roux
It is bound with whole eggs and baked
It uses clarified butter, not yolk
questions.why: Both are yolk emulsions, but mayonnaise is made cold with oil, while hollandaise is warm and made with butter.

questions.q: What is a dependable working amount of oil for each yolk in a mayonnaise?
questions.why: A working ratio of 150 to 250 ml a yolk leaves a margin; Escoffier's six yolks to a litre comes to about 165 ml each.

questions.q: Why is the oil added a drop at a time at the start?
distractors: The yolk must cook in the acid first
The mustard needs time to dissolve
It keeps the sauce from turning yellow
questions.why: Until the first droplets are coated and the sauce thickens, a stream of oil simply pools and the sauce never forms.

questions.q: A cook takes the yolk and oil straight from the fridge. What is the risk?
questions.answer: It is slow to take and may split
distractors: The yolk sets firm and scrambles
The mustard turns the sauce green
questions.why: A cold yolk emulsifies slowly and cold oil is thick and hard to divide into droplets, so the sauce breaks easily.

questions.q: A mayonnaise is too stiff before all the oil is in. What should go in next?
questions.answer: A few drops of water or lemon juice
distractors: Nothing: whisk harder until it loosens
A short rest in the fridge
questions.why: Stiffness means the water is running out; a few drops give the oil room to disperse before the stream resumes.

questions.q: Why do many cooks use extra virgin olive oil for only part of a mayonnaise?
questions.answer: Beaten hard, it can turn bitter
distractors: It will not emulsify with a yolk at all
questions.why: Extra virgin olive oil beaten hard, especially in a blender, can taste bitter, so a neutral oil carries most of the sauce.

questions.q: Which sauce is mayonnaise with tomato purée and fine strips of sweet red pepper?
questions.why: Andalouse adds tomato and sweet red pepper; verte is green with herbs, tartare carries pickles and chives, and béarnaise is a warm butter sauce.

questions.q: Besides flavour, what does a spoonful of mustard bring to a mayonnaise?
distractors: Heat that gently cooks the yolk
questions.why: Mustard's fine particles coat oil droplets alongside the yolk's lecithin, so the sauce takes more readily and holds.

questions.q: A mayonnaise has split into a thin, oily curdle. What is the usual rescue?
questions.answer: Whisk it slowly into a fresh yolk
distractors: Heat it gently until it thickens again
Pour in the rest of the oil quickly
Chill it hard, then whisk it again
questions.why: A fresh yolk, or a spoonful of water, gives the oil new water and emulsifier to spread into; added a drop at a time, the sauce rebuilds.

questions.q: Why do restaurant kitchens commonly make mayonnaise with pasteurised eggs?
questions.why: No cooking step kills bacteria in a mayonnaise, so kitchens start with eggs heated just enough to kill them without setting.
